topic: L1.2 Theoretical Foundations of Number Base Systems
subject: Maths

concepts.name: Place-Value Notation and Expansion
concepts.description: The foundational positional-system principle that every digit contributes face value times a power of the radix, with the radix point separating b^0 from b^-1. Questions ask for full place-value expansion of integers and fractions in bases 2, 5, and 16.
core_skills: Write any integer or fraction in base b as an expanded sum of digit × b^k, including negative powers
Evaluate an expanded form to a decimal value using positive and negative powers of the base
Identify the place value contributed by each digit position in bases 2, 5, 8, 10, and 16
Expand numbers like 204.13₅ into powers of 5 (2·5² + 0·5¹ + 4·5⁰ + 1·5⁻¹ + 3·5⁻²)
Convert a binary bicimal such as 1011.101₂ into decimal via full place-value expansion (11.625₁₀)
misconceptions: Treating fractional digits as decimal fractions (e.g., reading 0.32₅ as 3/10 + 2/100) instead of as powers of 5
Confusing a digit's face value with its place value, e.g., treating the hex digit B as 11 rather than 11 × 16¹ in 3B.4₁₆
traps: In base 5 the second fractional digit is 1/25 = 0.04, so 0.32₅ = 0.6 + 0.08 = 0.68₁₀; misplacing the negative power produces the distractor 0.64₁₀
Hexadecimal letter digits A–F must be replaced by 10–15 before place-value evaluation, so 3B.4₁₆ = 59.25₁₀ and 4C1₁₆ = 1217₁₀
concepts.depth_test: Explain why 0.32₅ = 0.68₁₀ and why 0.1101₂ = 13/16 by writing out the negative-power expansion rather than simply stating a converted result.

concepts.name: Integer Base Conversion
concepts.description: Converting whole numbers between decimal and another base: repeated division with reversed remainders for decimal→base, and polynomial evaluation of the positional expansion for base→decimal.
core_skills: Convert a decimal integer to base b by repeated division, reading remainders in reverse order (254₁₀ → FE₁₆, 1000₁₀ → 13000₅)
Convert a base-b integer to decimal by evaluating its place-value expansion (A3F₁₆, 4C1₁₆, 756₈ → 1EE₁₆ via intermediate pathways)
Express decimal integers in hexadecimal using letter digits for remainders of 10–15
prerequisites: Multiplication and division of whole numbers
misconceptions: Reading division remainders in the order they are produced instead of reversed (distractor EF₁₆ for 254₁₀ → FE₁₆)
Stopping the repeated-division chain too early or mishandling the final quotient, giving off-by-one results like FF₁₆
traps: Remainders 10–15 must be written as the letters A–F in hexadecimal, so 254₁₀ = FE₁₆, not E14₁₆
Repeated division must run until the quotient reaches 0; the final quotient becomes the leading digit (1000₁₀ = 13000₅)
concepts.depth_test: Explain why repeated division by the target base produces the digits of the answer in reverse order, using 254₁₀ → FE₁₆ or 1000₁₀ → 13000₅ as the worked example.

concepts.name: Fractional Base Conversion and Bicimals
concepts.description: Converting fractional parts between bases by repeated multiplication by the target base, and recognizing which fractions terminate and which recur in a given base.
core_skills: Convert a decimal fraction to a base-b bicimal by repeatedly multiplying by b and recording integer parts (0.625₁₀ → 0.101₂, 0.3125₁₀ → 0.24₈)
Convert a bicimal to a decimal fraction using negative powers and reduce to lowest terms (0.1101₂ → 13/16)
Find the binary representation of a fraction like 7/16 → 0.0111₂
Determine whether a fraction terminates or produces a recurring bicimal in a target base
misconceptions: Reading the generated fractional digits in reverse order, as in integer conversion, rather than in the order they are generated
Assuming a finite decimal fraction always has a finite binary representation (0.2₁₀ does not)
Multiplying by the wrong factor when the target base is not 2, e.g., using ×2 instead of ×8 for octal conversion
traps: 0.2₁₀ has no finite binary form; it repeats forever as 0.00110011...₂ because 1/5 cannot be written with a denominator that is a power of 2
A fraction terminates in base b only if its denominator divides some power of b; otherwise the repeating block must be identified and explained
0.3125₁₀ → 0.24₈ requires multiplying by 8, not by 2
concepts.depth_test: Explain why 0.625₁₀ terminates in binary while 0.2₁₀ recurs, and determine the binary representation of 7/16, justifying each fractional digit.

concepts.name: Power-Related Base Conversion (Binary ↔ Octal ↔ Hexadecimal)
concepts.description: Converting between bases that are powers of two by grouping digits into fixed-size blocks — nibbles of 4 bits for hex and triads of 3 bits for octal — working outward from the radix point.
core_skills: Convert binary to hexadecimal by grouping bits into 4-bit nibbles from the radix point (11010110₂ → D6₁₆)
Convert binary to octal by grouping bits into 3-bit triads from the radix point (10111001₂ → 271₈)
Convert hex or octal to binary by expanding each digit into its fixed bit block
Use binary as an intermediate pathway for octal-to-hexadecimal conversion (756₈ → 1EE₁₆)
State and apply the grouping theorem for converting from base b to base b^k
misconceptions: Grouping bits from the wrong end instead of starting at the radix point
Dropping leading zeros in the most-significant block, changing the leading output digit
Confusing block sizes — using 4 bits per octal digit or 3 bits per hex digit
traps: A3F₁₆ = 1010 0011 1111₂ must be regrouped as 101 000 111 111 → 5077₈; a single miscopied nibble changes the entire octal result
The leftmost incomplete block must be padded with leading zeros (10111001₂ → 010 111 001 → 271₈; 756₈ → 111 101 110 → 0001 1110 1110 → 1EE₁₆)
Converting base b to base b^k is valid only when the target base is a power of the source base
concepts.depth_test: Prove why grouping digits into blocks of size k converts a number from base b to base b^k, then use the method to convert 756₈ directly to hexadecimal.

concepts.name: Arithmetic in Non-Decimal Bases
concepts.description: Performing addition, subtraction, and multiplication entirely within a base, treating the radix b as the regrouping value for carries and borrows rather than converting to decimal.
core_skills: Add multi-digit numbers in base b with carries every time a column sum reaches b (342₅ + 423₅ = 1320₅)
Subtract binary numbers using binary borrows (11010₂ − 1011₂ = 1111₂)
Multiply in base b without converting to decimal (65₈ × 43₈ = 3477₈)
Add hexadecimal numbers with letter digits and carries (A7B₁₆ + 4E9₁₆ = F64₁₆)
prerequisites: Standard addition, subtraction, and multiplication algorithms
misconceptions: Adding columns as if they were base 10 and writing down digits that equal or exceed the base (the distractor 765₅ contains invalid digits 7 and 6)
Carrying at the wrong threshold, such as carrying at 10 in base 5 instead of at 5
Applying memorized decimal multiplication facts to a different base instead of recomputing each partial product in the base
traps: In base 5, a column summing to 12 is written as 2 with a carry of 2 (the number of times 5 goes into 12)
In hex addition, carries and letter-digit arithmetic combine: B + 9 = 20₁₀ = 14₁₆ writes 4 and carries 1
Every digit in the final answer must be strictly less than the base — an invalid digit signals an arithmetic error
concepts.depth_test: Perform 65₈ × 43₈ entirely in octal notation and explain the value of each carry produced, without converting the numbers to base 10.

concepts.name: Solving for Unknown Radix in Base Equations
concepts.description: Translating a numeral with an unknown base into a polynomial equation via positional expansion, then solving for the base and validating it against the digit constraints of the numeral.
core_skills: Expand a base-b numeral into a polynomial in the unknown base (35_b = 3b + 5, 123_x = x² + 2x + 3, 212_b = 2b² + b + 2)
Solve linear and quadratic equations for the base (35_b = 29₁₀ → b = 8; 123_x = 38₁₀ → x = 5; 212_b = 57₁₀ → b = 5)
Expand product equations digit-by-digit before solving (13_b × 12_b = 211_b → b = 5)
Reject inadmissible roots by checking that the base exceeds every digit in the numeral
misconceptions: Dropping the units digit when building the polynomial (solving 3b = 29 instead of 3b + 5 = 29)
Accepting the negative root of the quadratic as a valid base instead of discarding it
Forgetting that a valid base must be strictly greater than every digit appearing in the numeral
traps: For 123_x = 38₁₀, the polynomial x² + 2x + 3 = 38 factors as (x + 7)(x − 5); only x = 5 is admissible since the base must exceed the digit 3
Multi-digit factor multiplication must be done digit-by-digit in the base: 13_b × 12_b = (b + 3)(b + 2)
A candidate base that is smaller than or equal to any digit of the numeral is invalid by definition
concepts.depth_test: Solve 13_b × 12_b = 211_b for the positive integer base b and justify why the solution is the only admissible base, given the digits present.

concepts.name: Digit Validity and Radix Constraints
concepts.description: The rule that a base-b positional system uses exactly the digits 0 through b−1, making any digit equal to or greater than b invalid in that system.
core_skills: Identify invalid digits for a given base (7 is invalid in base 7, which uses only 0–6)
Check that every digit of a numeral is less than its stated base
Reject arithmetic or conversion results that contain invalid digits (e.g., 765₅)
misconceptions: Believing base 7 uses the digits 1 through 7 because decimal 10₁₀ is written with a 7 in one sense, rather than 0–6
Thinking the base equals the number of digits below it plus one in the wrong direction, e.g., that base 5 has five digits counting from 1
Treating large-looking digits like 7 as automatically valid without checking the radix
traps: A result such as 765₅ is self-evidently invalid because digits 7 and 6 are not allowed in base 5
When solving for an unknown base, the valid root must be greater than every digit of the original numeral (b > 6 required if the numeral contains digit 6)
The digit b−1 is the largest legal digit; digit b itself is never allowed
concepts.depth_test: Explain why 7 is an invalid digit in base 7 yet a perfectly valid digit in base 8, and why a computed base of 4 would be rejected for a numeral that contains the digit 6.

concepts.name: Fixed-Digit Bounds and Ranges
concepts.description: The counting formulas for n-digit fields in base b: b^n distinct values representable with n digits, maximum value b^n − 1, and minimum n-digit value b^(n−1).
core_skills: Compute the largest n-digit number in base b as b^n − 1 (largest 4-digit octal number = 4095₁₀)
Compute the number of distinct values representable with n digits as b^n (10-bit binary integer → 1024 values)
State and apply the formula for the smallest non-zero n-digit integer in base b as b^(n−1)
Compute differences between the largest and smallest n-digit numbers in a base (555₆ − 100₆ = 179₁₀)
Convert fixed-digit maximums to byte storage requirements (M(6,16) = 16,777,215₁₀ needs 3 bytes)
misconceptions: Confusing the count of representable values (b^n) with the maximum value (b^n − 1), producing the off-by-one distractor 4096 for a 4-digit octal field
Choosing the numeral itself (7777₈) instead of converting the largest value into the requested base
Confusing the smallest n-digit number (b^(n−1)) with zero or with b^n
traps: A 10-bit field stores 1024 distinct values but its maximum value is only 1023
The smallest 3-digit number in base 6 is 100₆ = 36₁₀, not 0, so largest − smallest = 215 − 36 = 179₁₀
16⁶ = 2²⁴ = 16,777,216, so the maximum 6-digit hex value 16,777,215 requires exactly 24 bits, which is 3 bytes
concepts.depth_test: Derive the formulas M(n,b) = b^n − 1 and N(n,b) = b^n, and explain the difference between the number of representable values and the maximum value for a 10-bit integer.

concepts.name: Divisibility Rules in Arbitrary Bases
concepts.description: The algebraic digit-sum rule that a base-b number is divisible by b−1 if and only if the sum of its digits is divisible by b−1, with the decimal Rule of 9s as the special case b = 10.
core_skills: Prove that abc_b = (b−1)[a(b+1) + b] + (a + b + c) by manipulating the positional expansion
State and apply the digit-sum divisibility test for b−1 in any base
Show that the decimal rule of 9s is the b = 10 instance of the general rule
misconceptions: Believing the divisibility-by-9 rule is a special property of decimal rather than a general b−1 phenomenon
Failing to separate the number into a multiple of (b−1) plus the digit sum during the proof
Applying the digit-sum rule to divisors other than b−1 without justification
traps: The proof works only because each power of b is congruent to 1 modulo (b−1); the rule does not generalize to arbitrary divisors
The analog in hexadecimal is divisibility by 15, and in octal it is divisibility by 7
The factor (b−1) must be pulled out explicitly from the full expansion, not just from the leading terms
concepts.depth_test: Write a formal algebraic proof that a 3-digit base-b number abc_b is divisible by b−1 whenever a + b + c is, and then demonstrate why the decimal rule of 9s is exactly the b = 10 case.

concepts.name: Radix Complement and Two's Complement
concepts.description: Representing negative integers in digital systems using the b's complement of the positive magnitude, with two's complement (invert all bits, then add 1) as the binary case.
core_skills: Explain the purpose and mechanism of radix complement for representing negative numbers
Compute an 8-bit two's complement by bitwise inversion followed by adding 1 (−45₁₀ → 11010011₂)
Work to a fixed field width, including leading zeros, before computing the complement
misconceptions: Omitting the final '+1' after bitwise inversion (which would give 11010010₂ instead of 11010011₂)
Using a sign-magnitude approach that merely flips the sign bit rather than computing the complement
Computing the complement to the wrong bit width
traps: −45₁₀ in 8-bit two's complement: 45 = 00101101₂ → invert to 11010010₂ → add 1 to get 11010011₂; skipping any step changes the value
The field width determines the leading zeros that must be inverted, so an 8-bit computation differs from a wider one
Two's complement is the radix complement of binary, not a sign-magnitude encoding
concepts.depth_test: Explain the concept of the b's complement for representing negative numbers in digital systems, then compute the 8-bit two's complement of −45₁₀ showing the inversion and '+1' steps.

concepts.name: Radix Economy and Optimal Base Selection
concepts.description: The theoretical efficiency trade-off between digit count and digit-set size, quantified as E(b,N) = b·log_b(N), which calculus shows is minimized at b = e ≈ 2.718, making ternary more efficient than binary.
core_skills: Set up the radix economy function E(b,N) = b·log_b(N) for representing a number N in base b
Minimize E with respect to b using differentiation, obtaining dE/db = 0 at b = e
Interpret why base 3, as the integer closest to e, is theoretically the most efficient base, ahead of binary
misconceptions: Minimizing the number of digits alone rather than the product of the base size and digit count
Assuming base 2 is theoretically optimal simply because binary is the standard in digital computers
Mishandling the derivative of b·log_b(N), which requires rewriting as b·ln(N)/ln(b)
traps: The derivative of E(b,N) = b·ln N / ln b vanishes when ln b = 1, i.e., at b = e ≈ 2.718
Among integer bases, base 3 is closest to e, so ternary beats binary in theoretical radix economy even though engineering factors favor binary
Radix economy is a theoretical cost metric, not a claim about hardware feasibility
concepts.depth_test: Prove using calculus that E(b,N) = b·log_b(N) is minimized at b = e, and explain why this result shows base 3 (ternary) is theoretically more efficient than base 2 (binary).
